submission.text:
The pie chart shows the regional distribution of Coca-Cola's unit case sales in 2000, while the line graph presents its share price between 1996 and 2001.

Overall, North America accounted for the largest share of sales, whereas Africa and the Middle East had the smallest proportion. The share price fluctuated considerably, reaching a peak around 1998 before declining.

Total sales amounted to 17.1 billion unit cases in 2000. North America represented 30.4% of this volume, followed by Latin America at 25.7%. Together, these two regions accounted for just over half of the total. Europe contributed a further 20.5%, while Asia's share stood at 16.4%. The remaining 7% came from Africa and the Middle East.

Turning to the share price, it began at approximately $35 and rose, with some fluctuations, to a high of roughly $80 in 1998. It then generally fell, dropping below $50 around 2000 before recovering to about $60. At the end of the period, the price was approximately $55, higher than at the beginning but well below its peak.

submission.text:
Universities are often expected to prepare students for employment, but they also have a responsibility to develop academic understanding. Both purposes are valuable, and I believe degree programmes should combine a strong academic foundation with opportunities to apply it.

Those who favour employment skills point to the difficulties graduates can face when entering the workplace. Knowing a subject does not automatically mean that someone can work effectively with colleagues or use the equipment required in a particular job. For example, engineering students might design a device for a local organisation, learning to manage deadlines while applying technical knowledge. Such experience can help them make informed career choices as well as demonstrate their abilities to employers. This is especially useful when students have had little contact with professional work before attending university.

However, concentrating only on immediate workplace requirements would narrow the value of higher education. Software, procedures and even entire occupations can change, whereas an understanding of underlying principles helps graduates adapt. Academic study also teaches students to question assumptions and assess evidence, which matters beyond any single career. A student who understands how research is conducted is better equipped to distinguish a persuasive claim from a reliable conclusion. These habits benefit both professional decisions and participation in public debate.

The most effective approach is therefore integration rather than a choice between these aims. The balance will vary by discipline, but neither element needs to displace the other. Graduates should leave with useful capabilities and the intellectual resources to continue learning when their first job changes.
